# Can behavior coders agree? Negative kappa on TutorMoments

Before predicting human behavior, a researcher must specify what counts as an event. A classifier can return perfectly valid JSON while disagreeing with another classifier about the meaning of an utterance. We tested a provisional codebook on actual tutoring dialogue with three automated coders. The results do not support adoption.

![Experiment overview](/assets/research/h28-cover.svg)

## Study design

Open coding builds categories inductively from observations. The [Tutor Move Taxonomy](https://www.alphaxiv.org/abs/2603.05778) proposes theory-aligned categories for instructional moves; a [2024 study of individual mathematics tutoring](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10639-024-13195-9) reports Cohen's kappa of 0.83 after training two human coders. Neither is a matched comparison to our automated coders.

We used [Ai2 TutorMoments-Preview](https://huggingface.co/datasets/allenai/tutormoments-preview), pinned revision 3bb0c104d65e29facffca7ba864ef10fa22d0e78, CC BY 4.0, for research only. The 462 real sessions were partitioned by student pseudonym into 132 training and 66 test groups. We counted provisional surface markers in 47,413 nonempty training utterances of at most 240 characters: question 7,749, explicit uncertainty 719, explanation 1,097, digit 933 and short acknowledgment 8,577. In 508 utterances, more than one marker matched. The categories were proposed in advance and checked against training frequencies, not discovered by fully inductive open coding.

We sampled one utterance from each of 48 held-out groups with a fixed seed and applied a regex coder and two local Qwen2.5 models, 0.5B and 1.5B. Six mutually exclusive labels were prioritized: question, explicit uncertainty, explanation, number, acknowledgment, other. The models received the utterance only and a structured output schema. No identity, demographic or future utterance was included. The target was observable language, not emotion, ability or diagnosis. The models share a family and are not independent human judges.

## Measuring agreement

![Coder label distributions](/assets/research/h28-labels.svg)

Fleiss' kappa corrects observed agreement for agreement expected from pooled label frequencies: (P_o-P_e)/(1-P_e). All 48 items had three valid labels. All 96 local model calls satisfied the output schema, but format validity does not establish semantic accuracy.

| Metric | Value |
|---|---:|
| Observed agreement | 0.361111 |
| Expected agreement | 0.411844 |
| Fleiss kappa | -0.086258 |

![Pairwise agreement](/assets/research/h28-agreement.svg)

Rule versus 0.5B agreed on 47.92%, rule versus 1.5B on 18.75%, and 0.5B versus 1.5B on 41.67%. The rule selected number zero times, compared with six and 23 times for the models. The rule requires a digit while the model description allows a numeric answer, so the operational definitions are not identical. This is a plausible contributor, not a proven error attribution. Without independent labels, no coder can be declared correct. Kappa here is a descriptive statistic of automated outputs, not population-level human agreement.

Human free-text student-behavior summaries exist for 52 sessions. Among 22 test-side sessions with summaries, only one has at least three distinct annotators, and the summaries do not implement our turn-level codebook. We therefore did not calculate a human three-rater kappa.

## Implications

Develop codes inductively on separate authorized training conversations, freeze boundary examples and inclusion criteria, and obtain sufficiently many common units rated blindly by independent qualified humans. Evaluate automated coders against those independent labels, with uncertainty and class-specific scores. Any revision informed by this diagnostic requires fresh evaluation data. No model promotion or product integration is justified. Remaining work is tracked in [issue #843](https://github.com/Daisuke134/anicca-ops/issues/843).

The corpus includes minors and was used in earlier research. We export aggregate counts and reproduction code only, not utterances, IDs, individual predictions or weights.
